To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(a) Korean speakers (KS) mention more specific subjects at long presentation durations whereas English speakers (ESs) are more likely to do so at short presentation durations; (b) ESs are more likely to mention more background details at longer durations; (c) KSs recall background details more accurately.
the language speakers’ choice of subject referent is not affected by presentation duration and that the language speakers are more accurate in recalling background details than foreground figures.

Korean speakers’ verbalizations were more influenced by time, that English speakers’ utterances were not, that Korean speakers’ recall of background details was better than English speakers’, and that English speakers’ recall of figures was better than Korean speakers’ recall.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the question of how the language speakers’ perceptual orientations are shaped by the language they speak.
the relationship between verbalization patterns, attentional orientation, and recall performance.
the question how language shapes perception and cognition.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the differences between the two languages are not only in their syntactic structure, but also in their cognitive and cultural underpinnings.
Korean is more background-oriented than English.
Korean speakers’ verbalization is more sensitive to presentation duration than English speakers’.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the differences between Korean and English speakers’ verbalization patterns and recall accuracy were more likely to be caused by the differences in the language speakers’ cognitive processing strategies than by the differences in language structures.

the differences in language structure and usage patterns between Korean and English are reflected in their visual scene description and recall, and that the differences in the two languages have implications for second language learning.
the language speakers’ verbalization patterns reflect their perceptual preferences, and the perceptual orientations in turn influence the speakers’ memory for the depicted scenes.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the language-specific encoding patterns are not only determined by the language structure but also by the language users’ perceptual orientations.
language-specific verbalization patterns are not necessarily the result of the differences in the language structure but may be the product of language speakers’ perceptual orientation.
a language’s grammatical features may not be the only factors that influence the speakers’ verbalization patterns.
